entry.title: The article a CII president will write in 2047: A roadmap for industry
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / The article a CII president will write in 2047: A roadmap for industryThe article a CII president will write in 2047: A roadmap for industry

From deeper domestic capabilities to international competitiveness, here are 6 priorities for industry

premium

Illustration: Binay Sinha

R Mukundan5 min read Last Updated : Nov 24 2026 | 9:29 PM ISTSometime in August 2047, as India marks 100 years of Independence, a president of the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII) may write in this newspaper and the article could read something like this:  “India enters its second century of freedom as a developed economy. Average incomes have reached high-income levels, manufacturing contributes a quarter of national output, and Indian companies are global leaders in pharmaceuticals, specialised materials, electronics, semiconductors and clean energy technologies.  Made in India has become synonymous with quality. Indian businesses invest substantially in research, own valuable intellectual property and compete internationally. Most working Indians have formal jobs with rising wages, women’s workforce participation has risen, and small suppliers have become global competitors.  None of this was inevitable. It was built, decision by decision, from the middle of the 2020s.”  That article remains unwritten. The distance between this hypothetical future and where we stand today defines the task before us.  India’s per capita gross national income was $2,760 in 2025, against the World Bank’s high-income threshold of over $14,375. Manufacturing contributes around 15 per cent of gross value added, while research and development (R&D) expenditure is approximately 0.84 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP), less than half from business. Women’s labour force participation remains below men’s. These figures are not a criticism of our progress, but a measure of the transformation still required.  Over the past 12 years, the government has laid strong foundations for this journey. Sustained infrastructure investment, goods and services tax, digital public infrastructure, Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, corporate tax reforms, production linked incentive schemes and trade agreements have strengthened India’s economic capabilities. The Reserve Bank of India and the Securities and Exchange Board of India have contributed to financial stability, deeper capital markets and investor confidence. The consistency of reforms, despite global shocks, has mattered. Equally, continued reform will be necessary as technology, markets and global competition evolve.  The results are visible. Smartphones emerged as India’s largest individual export item in FY26. As many as 12 semiconductor projects have been approved. Non-fossil power capacity crossed 300 gigawatts in July 2026. India’s investment rate reached 34.5 per cent of GDP in FY25, while CII’s Private Investment Barometer records private project announcements of ~26.6 trillion during April-September 2026 — 86 per cent from private firms.  These are considerable achievements, but they represent the foundations of India’s transformation, not its completion. Sustained growth of around 8 per cent over the coming decades will require the government and industry to build on them with greater ambition.  For a CII President in 2047 to write the article imagined above, Indian industry must accomplish six things.  First, invest ahead of demand. The Prime Minister’s call to place India First in long-term investment decisions is particularly relevant. Today’s investment pipeline is encouraging, but the real test is how quickly announcements become productive capacity, and whether they create competitive enterprises.  Second, build depth alongside scale. India manufactures medicines but imports many critical ingredients, assembles electronics with imported components and remains dependent on overseas suppliers for advanced materials. Industry must progressively develop domestic capabilities in design, engineering, technology and higher-value components, competitively rather than through permanent protection.  Third, invest in knowledge. India’s ambitions cannot be realised with present levels of business R&D. Companies must invest more in research, strengthen partnerships with universities, develop indigenous technologies and build globally competitive intellectual property.  Fourth, translate productivity into prosperity. A developed economy requires productive employment and rising wages. Industry must expand apprenticeships, invest in continuous workforce training, create greater opportunities for women and ensure that technological progress benefits workers as well.  Fifth, compete for the world. India’s domestic market of 1.4 billion people must become a platform for global competitiveness, not a shelter from it. Companies must meet international quality standards, use trade agreements effectively and develop products for markets in developed and emerging economies.  Sixth, take smaller enterprises along. Large companies must strengthen supplier ecosystems through technology partnerships, quality certification, predictable procurement and timely payments. India’s industrial competitiveness will ultimately depend on the capabilities of thousands of MSMEs, not only its largest companies.  None of these tasks can be accomplished by industry or the government acting independently. The two sides will naturally have their own perspectives on specific issues, and these may produce headlines more dramatic than the discussions warrant. But we should not allow the headlines of the day to distract us from our shared task. The government has demonstrated what sustained reform can achieve. Industry must demonstrate what sustained investment, innovation and enterprise can deliver.  Together, we must also move from ease of doing business to speed of doing business. As global supply chains are reconfigured, the time taken to approve investments, build facilities and commence production increasingly determines competitiveness. States will have a particularly important role in accelerating progress on land, power, approvals and labour.  CII intends to contribute through its councils, centres of excellence, skills initiatives and nationwide network, working with members on these six priorities and measuring progress against tangible outcomes, year after year.  The CII President writing in 2047 should be able to look back at this period as the time when the government and industry, working as Team Bharat, converted India’s economic potential into lasting prosperity.”  What that President writes then will depend on what we do now. I would like that article to be written.  
The writer is the president of CII   Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. They do not necessarily reflect the opinion of www.business-standard.com or the Business Standard newspaperTopics : CII BS Opinion Development economic growth

entry.title: India should pursue US trade deal and widen export options for firms
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / India should pursue US trade deal and widen export options for firmsIndia should pursue US trade deal and widen export options for firms

India should pursue a trade deal with the US while safeguarding its interests and addressing tariff disadvantages through market diversification and export competitiveness

premium

India-US trade negotiations amid proposed US tariff increases on Indian goods (Representative Image)

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 26 2026 | 9:22 PM ISTThe United States (US) has proposed imposing up to a 25 per cent tariff on Indian goods but offered to lower it to 17 per cent if both sides conclude a trade deal. This follows investigation by the United States Trade Representative (USTR) into alleged excess industrial capacity among trading partners. The investigation covered 14 economies, including India, along with China, Vietnam, Bangladesh and Japan. The proposed 25 per cent tariff on India will be net of existing Section 301 tariffs, while certain goods will remain exempt. India now faces 10 per cent tariffs along with regular Customs rates. A 25 per cent tariff will put India at a disadvantage because only Vietnam will attract a higher rate. However, a trade deal will give India a mild tariff advantage over countries such as Cambodia, Thailand, Indonesia and Malaysia. In the Indian context, the objective is to push for a deal.  The Indian government has taken the right stand by rejecting the claims of structural excess capacity and added that any trade-related concerns should be dealt with within the framework of the deal being negotiated between the two countries. The government is reported to be examining the notice issued by the USTR and will likely respond in due course. Trade relations with the US have been uncertain since the beginning of the second Donald Trump administration. The Trump administration imposed the so-called reciprocal tariffs on most countries early last year, including 26 per cent on India. These were later suspended and then reimposed at a 25 per cent rate. India was also subjected to punitive tariffs for importing Russian crude oil. It was removed only after both sides reached an agreement in February this year.  It is worth noting that the US Congress has done its bit to empower the country’s President to impose punitive tariffs on countries importing Russian energy. Given that India has been importing Russian crude oil, the threat of additional tariffs remains a real risk. Notably, despite the odds, according to the USTR data, India’s goods exports to the US in 2025 grew by about 19 per cent and crossed $100 billion, with a trade surplus of $58.4 billion. It is worth noting that relations with the US are much deeper than what the trade numbers suggest and need to be preserved. The Indian government has engaged with the US administration, and both sides have often communicated that the deal was almost done. However, it appears that the final agreement could not be reached. Since India now has deeper trade agreements with the United Kingdom and the European Union, the usual arguments about India’s unwillingness to open up its markets in such negotiations have been considerably weakened. Thus, it is unclear what is holding up the trade deal. One reason reportedly is the shifting US demands, which is possibly making the final agreement difficult for India. Nevertheless, India needs to keep engaging with the US and aim to conclude the trade deal at the earliest without compromising on its interests.  Broadly, India has done well to enter into various other trade agreements, which will help exporters in the country diversify and gain competitiveness. However, for this to happen in the desired way, the government must create an enabling environment and handhold industry, particularly small businesses, to overcome non-tariff requirements or barriers in the destination countries and regions. This will also help overcome some tariff disadvantages in the US if the deal gets delayed, though the objective should be to conclude it as quickly as possible.     Topics : Donald Trump India US Trade Deal US tariffs India exports Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

entry.title: SpiceJet disruptions show why aviation competition needs accountability
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / SpiceJet disruptions show why aviation competition needs accountabilitySpiceJet disruptions show why aviation competition needs accountability

The recent aberrations related to SpiceJet reflect the airline's indifference in a deeply consumer-facing industry

premium

SpiceJet, which had a domestic market share of around 15 per cent in 2019, is left with just 0.6 per cent as of September this year (Photo: Shutterstock)

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 26 2026 | 9:08 PM ISTThe recent flight cancellations and operational disruption at SpiceJet have caused considerable inconvenience to passengers. Widespread instances of a lack of communication and prior information on flight-time changes or cancellations have once again shown the Indian aviation sector in a poor light. Even as aviation in the country is dominated by two players, with IndiGo and Air India covering over 90 per cent of the domestic passenger market, the presence of other airlines holding the remaining 9-10 per cent has ensured that the sector does not slip into a duopoly. Indeed, competition is critical for any industry to thrive and a duopoly could put at risk the advantages that multiple players bring to the ecosystem. However, any worthwhile competition has to have its skin in the game and be accountable to consumers and the regulator.  The recent aberrations related to SpiceJet reflect the airline’s indifference in a deeply consumer-facing industry. While the regulator —Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) — sent a show-cause notice to the airline last week on the operational chaos and lack of compliance, it needs to act more decisively to put the house in order. The DGCA can impose financial penalties, address customer grievances through compensation, and even restrict the operations of any errant airline. There have been several instances of safety lapse as well as operational mismanagement over the recent months involving other airlines — Air India and IndiGo — as well. The regulator should be empowered further so that it can function with greater autonomy and independence when it comes to consumer protection.   SpiceJet, which had a domestic market share of around 15 per cent in 2019, is left with just 0.6 per cent as of September this year. At the beginning of the year, it had close to 4 per cent. The remarkable slide in the airline’s market share is a consequence of its worsening financial condition. According to reports, just seven of its 12 aircraft are operational this month, a situation that could take away many of its international and domestic airport slots. The DGCA has observed that SpiceJet does not meet the minimum fleet-eligibility requirements for scheduled international operations. According to the rules specified by the Ministry of Civil Aviation, an airline must deploy at least 20 aircraft or 20 per cent of its capacity (average number of seats across all departures), whichever is higher, on domestic operations to be eligible for international scheduled operations.  There are reports of other airlines eyeing SpiceJet’s international traffic rights in important hubs such as Dubai and Bangkok if the Ajay Singh-led carrier loses the bilateral entitlements related to its overseas flights and slots. However, there is no mechanism for an airline-to-airline transfer of traffic rights and any redistribution would require government decision under the applicable bilateral framework. SpiceJet, which continued to sell tickets, including on flights facing disruption, has said it’s going for a ₹5,500 crore fund-raising process after getting approval from the board recently. Since fund-raising is typically a lengthy process, there has to be an alternative plan in place to ensure that passengers don’t get short shrift until the airline gets sufficient liquidity to fly with confidence again.This is especially true with geopolitical turbulence forcing longer routes and rising prices of jet fuel making aviation a tough business to be in.     Topics : SpiceJet Aviation sector DGCA flight Flight ticket cancellations

entry.title: Digital payments fraud safeguards must come with banks' accountability
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Digital payments fraud safeguards must come with banks' accountabilityDigital payments fraud safeguards must come with banks' accountability

RBI's proposed safeguards give customers greater control over digital payments, but banks must remain accountable for preventing fraud and compensating victims

premium

The rapid adoption of digital payments has made financial transactions more seamless, but has also increased the risks of fraud

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 25 2026 | 10:23 PM ISTThe Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI’s) recent draft amendment directions on preventive safeguards for electronic-banking transactions are an important step to prevent fraud-related losses. The proposals allow customers to set transaction limits, disable payment channels, and activate a “stop switch” to block future customer-initiated debits. The stop switch could be particularly useful when customers suspect that their accounts or devices have been compromised. It would block customer-initiated debits, new payment mandates, and registration of their accounts on new third-party Unified Payments Interface (UPI) applications, while allowing incoming credits. Certain existing recurring mandates and bank-initiated debits, including loan instalments and charges, would remain outside its scope. A trusted-person mechanism, which will be voluntary, will introduce an additional layer of authentication for high-value transfers.  The proposals build on a series of regulatory steps taken this year. In February, the RBI had said it would issue a discussion paper exploring calibrated safeguards in digital payments, such as lagged credits and additional authentication for specific classes of users like senior citizens. These ideas were set out in its April discussion paper. In June, amendments to the customer-liability framework for fraudulent electronic-banking transactions expanded protections, strengthened complaint resolution, and provided compensation for small-value frauds. The latest draft directions take this agenda further by giving customers greater control over how and to what extent digital-payment channels can be used.  The rapid adoption of digital payments has made financial transactions more seamless, but has also increased the risks of fraud. Digital arrests alone reportedly generated over 21,900 complaints, involving more than ₹647 crore, between January and August this year. Phishing, impersonation and coercion can manipulate customers into authorising transactions themselves, while money routed through mule accounts can disappear before complaints are processed. Customer controls alone cannot address all these vulnerabilities. Banks must invest in real-time detection of unusual transaction patterns, suspicious-account monitoring, rapid fund-freezing protocols, and effective coordination across banks, payment intermediaries, and law-enforcement agencies. The Supreme Court, while recently hearing a digital-arrest matter, pushed for banks to identify transactions inconsistent with customers’ past behaviour, temporarily suspend suspicious transfers, and compensate victims where failures in due diligence contribute to losses. This rightly shifts scrutiny towards banks rather than treating every fraud as customer negligence.  The RBI’s proposed expansion of the definition of “bank negligence” is, therefore, significant. It covers failures to implement authentication safeguards, issue mandatory transaction alerts, respond promptly to complaints, block channels after repeated failed authentication attempts, and implement customer-selected controls. System failures, security breaches, and employee or third-party collusion that facilitate fraud would also fall within the definition. Victims should not bear the financial consequences of institutional lapses. Grievance redress must be faster and more transparent, with clear timelines for investigating fraud, recovering funds, and deciding compensation. Banks must also ensure that the proposed safeguards can be activated quickly and easily. A secure digital-payment ecosystem cannot be built just by asking customers to be more vigilant. The proposals are a welcome step towards giving customers greater control, but the regulator must ensure that banks remain accountable for preventing fraud, responding swiftly when it occurs, and compensating victims when their own failures contribute to losses.     Topics : RBI digital payment UPI Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

entry.title: Nvidia saga exposes succession and governance risks for founder-led firms
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Nvidia saga exposes succession and governance risks for founder-led firmsNvidia saga exposes succession and governance risks for founder-led firms

Nvidia's leadership controversy highlights the risks of weak succession planning, political interference and excessive dependence on promoter CEOs

premium

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang | Image: Bloomberg

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 25 2026 | 10:17 PM ISTJensen Huang’s reinstatement as chief executive officer (CEO) of Nvidia has raised many questions about corporate governance and national security in the United States (US), and political interference in what should strictly be a corporate decision. The legal and reputational risks centre on Nvidia. However, the risks concerning national security and the US President Donald Trump’s involvement could lead to far wider consequences. The controversial decision by Nvidia’s board appears influenced by Mr Trump’s explicit desire to see Mr Huang back in charge. Mr Trump is reported to have a personal stake worth over $60 million in Nvidia. At the same time, the White House has blacklisted Megaspeed, the company founded by Alice Huang, the Chinese national with whom Mr Huang had a liaison. The lady is alleged to be a Chinese asset who may have wheedled secrets out of Mr Huang and enabled China to access high-end Nvidia chips.  Apart from security considerations, one of the concerns for investors is the lack of a succession plan. The world’s most valuable semiconductor manufacturer was (and remains) a one-man show, despite being a $4 trillion behemoth. Over 50 departments directly reported to Mr Huang. Since he didn’t believe in succession plans, his departure left Nvidia with a vacuum at the top. This concentration of responsibilities is usual in startups. But it is also the case in many tech companies that have moved quickly into the big league. The market valuations of SpaceX and Tesla, for example, are inextricably linked to Elon Musk’s personal actions. So is that of Meta, where Mark Zuckerberg has tight control of voting rights. Players in artificial intelligence (AI) such as OpenAI and Anthropic, valued in trillions, have similar issues, given that they are run by a few high-profile individuals.  In such cases, actions by the CEO (the actions that don’t directly impinge on operations) may lead to big swings in perceptions. However, as seen with Google, Microsoft and Apple, startups that grow at dizzying speed can also evolve to being run in a more conventional fashion, diluting the association of a company’s brand with an individual. Mr Huang’s return may seem to have kicked the succession issue down the road, but that’s not really true, given the overhang of national-security considerations and accusations that the President has interfered in the matter because of his interests. There was bipartisan condemnation of the reinstatement by the Republicans and Democrats. Mr Huang is scheduled to testify in front of Congress committees in January. By then, the Democrats will control both Houses of Congress and national-security considerations will be probed at length in those hearings. Many Republicans who are hardliners in their attitude to China may in this case be willing to go along with the Democrats. In that case, the reinstatement could have very far-reaching consequences.  The stock has seesawed as the saga played out. The retirement plans of many Americans are tied to Nvidia’s market value due to the structure of the US 401K retirement plan. Their net worth would have been significantly impacted by Mr Huang’s peccadillos. In India too, the emergence of an equity and mutual-fund culture has led to the net worth of many households being tied to market moves. The branding of many Indian companies is tightly linked in public perception to their promoter CEOs, and most also don’t have clear succession plans. India may see similar risks proliferating unless this event encourages corporations to consider setting such plans in place.     Topics : Nvidia Jensen Huang corporate governance CEO succession planning

entry.title: Nepal PM's India visit signals a thaw, but key demands remain unmet
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Nepal PM's India visit signals a thaw, but key demands remain unmetNepal PM's India visit signals a thaw, but key demands remain unmet

Balendra Shah's first state visit to India signals a thaw in bilateral ties, but differences over infrastructure, air connectivity and financial assistance remain.

premium

Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah's first state visit to India has opened the door to improving bilateral ties, with agreements on infrastructure, energy and trade, though differences over air connectivity and financial assistance persist. (Photo: PTI)

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 24 2026 | 11:44 PM ISTNepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah’s first state visit to India has offered an opportunity to reset relations, which have been unsettled for almost a decade. In choosing India, not China, for his first bilateral visit — unlike what his communist predecessor K P Oli did — Mr Shah signalled a willingness to overlook tensions to restore traditional ties. Significantly, China had extended an invitation to Mr Shah soon after he took office but preparations for a trip to Beijing were reportedly put on hold. The two-day visit offered New Delhi an opportunity to closely assess a leader who emerged from outside Nepal’s machine politics on the back of student protests and who has indicated a desire to be treated on an equal footing by his northern and southern neighbours with his “Nepal First” agenda.  The reorientation of relations was evident in the fact that both nations chose to set aside competing boundary claims, which flared up in May this year after Kathmandu objected to India using the disputed Lipulekh pass as a pilgrimage route to Kailash Mansarovar. Instead, Mr Shah and Prime Minister Narendra Modi underscored age-old civilisational links between the two Hindu-majority nations by virtually flagging off the Saryu-Kamala Express between Ayodhya and Janakpur, Nepal. Overall, however, the contours of the joint vision document, the eight bilateral agreements, and the development and infrastructure package suggest that India has chosen to be relatively conservative in meeting Nepal’s requirements. At the centre of the talks is India’s pledge of $1.6 billion for an economic and reconstruction assistance package following the devastating floods  caused by the collapse of a mountain glacier in August, killing about 1,500 people. The package includes a grant of $377 million for post-disaster and new infrastructure projects and a $1.24 billion line of credit for energy projects. The latter component reflects the damage caused by the floods, wiping out nearly 10 per cent of Nepal’s power-generation capacity, forcing it to turn to India to meet domestic demand. Given that Kathmandu has estimated rebuilding costs at $4.8 billion, there are indications that Nepal’s ruling regime would have preferred a larger commitment from India. Nepal, however, secured access to two ports — Kandla and Paradip — in addition to the existing rights at Kolkata, Haldia and Visakhapatnam — to conduct third-country trade, vital for a landlocked country.  An aviation agreement also partly fell short of Nepal’s expectations. Nepal has sought access to Indian airspace to attract international traffic to Bhairahawa and Pokhara, which serve as gateways to Lumbini (the Buddha’s birthplace) and the Himalayas, respectively. Both airports were built at high cost and incur heavy losses. But India has so far balked at permitting connectivity to these airports because they were built by Chinese state-owned contractors. New Delhi did, however, make bidirectional an existing air route linking Kathmandu, Bhairahawa and Lucknow, pending discussion over technical detail. Overall however, eight months into office, Mr Shah has made creditable gains with Nepal’s largest trading partner. Building on them will be his first big test in international relations.   Topics : Narendra Modi BS Opinion Business Standard Editorial Comment India Nepal ties Nepal Power generation

entry.title: Fertiliser subsidy reform must go beyond sharing costs with states
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Fertiliser subsidy reform must go beyond sharing costs with statesFertiliser subsidy reform must go beyond sharing costs with states

Sharing the urea subsidy burden with states may ease Centre's finances, but pricing distortions, import dependence and inefficient nutrient use require deeper reforms.

premium

India's fertiliser subsidy regime faces mounting fiscal pressure, but shifting part of the urea subsidy burden to states may not resolve pricing distortions, import dependence and inefficient nutrient use.

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 24 2026 | 9:59 PM ISTThe Union government is considering converting the urea subsidy into a centrally sponsored scheme (CSS), requiring states to share the expenditure, as reported by this newspaper. This reflects the growing pressure on government finances from India’s fertiliser-subsidy regime. Discussion is reportedly still at an early stage, with possible cost-sharing arrangements of 70:30, 60:40 or even 50:50 between the Centre and the states. The rationale is to reduce the Centre’s fiscal burden while making states more accountable for fertiliser distribution and curbing diversion for non-agricultural use. However, transferring expenditure will not address the structural problems.  The fiscal pressure is considerable. The Centre had budgeted ₹1.71 trillion for fertiliser subsidies in 2026-27, but had spent around 86 per cent of it by November 16. Urea accounts for approximately 68 per cent of the budgeted subsidy. Expenditure on imported urea had reached ₹43,246 crore against a re-appropriated allocation of ₹44,001 crore. The Fertiliser Association of India (FAI) has estimated that the subsidy bill this financial year could rise to ₹2.5 trillion, 46 per cent above the budgeted amount. This is despite an expected decline in fertiliser consumption to 65 million-67 million tonnes from 70 million tonnes last year. The numbers underline that the subsidy burden is not simply a consequence of excessive consumption or diversion; global price volatility and import dependence are also important drivers. There is a case for greater state involvement in monitoring fertiliser distribution. States are better positioned to oversee local supply chains, identify unusual purchases, and prevent subsidised urea from reaching industrial users. However, there are limits to this argument. If the Centre continues to determine retail prices, subsidy rates, and procurement arrangements, the states will be forced to share expenditure without corresponding decision-making powers. It could also disproportionately burden fiscally weaker states, particularly those with large agricultural requirements.  More importantly, the proposed arrangement does little to correct the distortions in fertiliser pricing. Urea is sold at a fixed price of ₹267 for a 45-kg bag, with the Centre compensating manufacturers for the difference between the cost of production or import and the retail price. This makes nitrogen substantially cheap relative to phosphorus and potassium, encouraging excessive urea application and an imbalance in nutrient consumption. In this context, extending the nutrient-based subsidy (NBS) regime to urea deserves consideration. Under the NBS regime, subsidies are linked to individual nutrients rather than the cost of supplying a particular product. This could help rationalise relative nutrient prices and encourage balanced fertiliser use.  However, the transition needs careful calibration to prevent abrupt increases in farmers’ input costs. At the same time, cost sharing will not insulate public finances from international price shocks. India needs to strengthen domestic production, diversify import sources, and improve nutrient-use efficiency. Better monitoring through digital tracking and point-of-sale systems is equally important to curb diversion without creating another layer of administrative complexity. The fertiliser subsidy regime needs deeper reforms. Shifting part of the expenditure will not address the fundamental problems.   Topics : Centrally sponsored schemes BS Opinion Business Standard Editorial Comment Fertilizers fertiliser subsidy urea subsidy

entry.title: RBI has already answered its own listing question in case of Tata Sons
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / RBI has already answered its own listing question in case of Tata SonsRBI has already answered its own listing question in case of Tata Sons

Tata Sons met public-company standards without selling shares. The regulator's own rules show that transparency needs no listing

premium

The regulator itself admits, in writing, that listed-company transparency is possible without listing. That is where this debate belongs

Nitin Potdar5 min read Last Updated : Nov 24 2026 | 9:26 PM ISTRegulators rarely answer their own questions. However, on listing large non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) already has.  Since June 2026, an NBFC with assets of ₹1 trillion and more is regarded as an “upper layer” (RBI NBFC: Registration Directions, 2025, para 24). Further, such an NBFC “shall be mandatorily listed within three years” of being identified. And disclosures “shall be put in place on the same lines as applicable to a listed company even before the actual listing” (RBI NBFC: Governance Directions, 2025, para 43).  The RBI goes further. An unlisted upper-layer NBFC must adopt a board-approved roadmap to meet the Securities and Exchange Board of India’s (Sebi’s) listing disclosure rules (RBI NBFC Financial Statements: Directions, 2025, para 23). Even an ordinary unlisted NBFC is asked to publish a corporate governance report on the lines of Sebi’s listing obligations and disclosure requirements regulations (same directions, para 22(7)).  The regulator has said, in writing, that listed-company transparency can be achieved without listing. That is where the debate should begin.  What is left for listing to do? Is it information for the regulator?  The RBI needs no stock exchange. It can demand any statement: Capital, borrowings, investments, every borrower, every loan and its interest rate (RBI Act, s. 45L(1)(a) and (2)).  Is it for governance? The RBI already mandates audit and nomination and remuneration committees (RBI NBFC: Governance Directions, 2025, paras 17-18), a chief risk officer (paras 19), a chief compliance officer (para 25) and limits on independent directors (para 27). It also has caps on lending to any one group. None of this depends on a listing.  Listing adds nothing to how an NBFC is regulated. It changes only who owns it.  Indian company law has never equated public accountability with listing. Under the Companies Act, 1956, certain large private companies were “deemed public companies” (s. 43A). They bore the scrutiny of a public company without being made to list. Tata Sons was one of them. For years it met public-company standards; the law never asked it to sell shares to the public. It returned to private status in 2017, and the Supreme Court upheld that in 2021. Why can’t the RBI treat Tata Sons as deemed public?  RBI on listing  If listing were essential to safety, the RBI would apply it to all. It does not.  An upper-layer NBFC “fully owned and controlled by the government” is neither to list nor to make pre-listing disclosures (RBI NBFC: Governance Directions, 2025, proviso to para 43. They carry every other upper-layer obligation. Only listing is waived.  Further, certain NBFCs in a bank’s group must follow upper-layer regulations “other than the requirement of listing” (RBI NBFC: Registration Directions, 2025, para 36A, Explanation). The full rulebook, without the listing.  Most importantly, an upper-layer company can exit without ever listing: By shrinking, by a board-approved restructuring (RBI NBFC: Registration Directions, 2025, para 29), or by giving up public funds.  The risk goes. So does the listing requirement.  A safeguard that the RBI can waive, and a company can walk away from, protects no one. It is a choice of policy.  Is ownership the RBI’s business? The regulator’s power over NBFCs comes from Chapter III-B of the RBI Act, written to protect those who lend money to these companies.  Its main power covers income recognition, accounting standards, provisioning, capital adequacy, deployment of funds and lending limits (RBI Act, s. 45JA). Every item concerns the balance sheet.  The other power covers “conduct of business” (s. 45L(1)(b)): How a company lends, not who owns it. Even this requires the RBI to have “due regard to the conditions in which, and the objects for which, the institution has been established” (s. 45L(3)). One rule for every large NBFC gives no such regard.  Compare banks. When the RBI grants a private banking licence, the conditions are written in at the start: List within a set period and bring the promoters’ stake down over time. Every promoter knows this before investing a rupee. An NBFC gets no such warning. It may have been built over decades with private capital, long before any layered framework existed. Then it crosses a size threshold and is told to sell itself to the public.  A bank accepts dilution as the price of entry. An NBFC is made to pay it after the fact.  Way out and way back  There is a final irony. Listing is not even permanent. Sebi’s rules allow a listed company to delist (Sebi (Delisting of Equity Shares) Regulations, 2021). So, is the plan for Tata Sons to list, and then apply to delist? Why force such a somersault: Sell shares to the public, make it buy them back at a premium and put a century of philanthropy at risk on the way?  Keep everything that makes these companies safe: Capital, exposure limits, independent boards and full listed-company disclosure. Then accept that disclosure as compliance, as the Act already allows (RBI Act, s. 45NC). And treat Tata Sons as deemed public.  Globally, Denmark, Germany and Switzerland settled this long ago. Novo Nordisk, Carlsberg, Bosch and Rolex are owned or controlled by foundations, and their governments protect the model rather than question it.  Earlier this month, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman urged an amicable settlement, calling Tata group “a very critical component to the Indian economy”. An amicable settlement surely cannot mean dismantling what the nation celebrates as the Tata model.

entry.title: For tariff classification, section and chapter titles have no legal force
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / For tariff classification, section and chapter titles have no legal forceFor tariff classification, section and chapter titles have no legal force

Expert answers on customs classification, FEMA reporting rules and duty-free re-export procedures for businesses

premium

Representative image for import-export

TNC Rajagopalan3 min read Last Updated : Nov 23 2026 | 11:05 PM ISTI refer to your article ‘Scotch at the Docks’, which appeared on November 16, where you have mentioned about the classification 21069051 for compound alcoholic preparations. I don’t understand why that item is under Chapter 21, which is for ‘miscellaneous edible preparations’, whereas there is a separate chapter 22 specifically for ‘beverages, spirits and vinegar’. Please clarify.  Rule 1 of the General Rules for Interpretation of the First Schedule to the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 says that “the titles of sections, chapters and sub-chapters are provided for ease of reference only; for legal purposes, classification shall be determined according to the terms of the headings and any relative section or chapter notes”. So, for classification, please do not go by the chapter or section titles only. Please go by the wording of the headings, subheadings and tariff items read with the relevant section and chapter notes and where necessary, the Interpretative Notes.   Secondly, please note that the tariff item 21069051 expressly covers qualifying ‘compound alcoholic preparations of a kind used to manufacture beverages’ and not the beverages. The distinction is between a preparation used to make a beverage and a beverage classifiable under Chapter 22.  I refer to your article ‘New FEMA rules bring small service exporters into the reporting net’ which appeared on November 4, wherein you have said that “even small service providers like individuals engaged in online teaching of music and yoga are required to furnish form EDF to the bank”. Our bankers say that it is not necessary to do so. Can you please clarify.  The position stated in my October 4, 2026 article was correct under the regulations as they stood on that date. The Reserve Bank of India subsequently amended Regulation 3(2) by a notification dated November 2, 2026, effective from October 1, 2026. Under the amended rule, a resident individual exporting services is deemed to have furnished the EDF upon giving the authorised dealer the information it requires to credit the inward re­mittance.   Your bankers are therefore right under the amended regulations. A separate EDF is unnecessary.  We had exported certain goods by claiming duty drawback and RoDTEP duty credits. Soon after exporting, we found that we had packed the goods wrongly and so, recalled the consignment for repacking and re-export. Now, we cannot use the notification 158/95-Cus dated November 14, 1995, because that is for repairs, reconditioning, reprocessing. Use of S. No.1 of notification no. 45/2017-Cus dated  June 30, 2017 would involve surrender of the export benefits and after Customs clearance and repacking, sending the goods as a fresh export claiming the benefits afresh. Is there a better way?  Yes. A warehousing route is available. File an into-bond bill of entry and move the goods to a bonded warehouse where you can ask for permission to repack the goods  for exports. After repacking, you can re-export the goods under Section 69 without payment of import duty, subject to its conditions, by filing an ex-bond shipping bill. In this route, you need not surrender any export benefits availed.

entry.title: India's mass incomes need small business growth, not just corporate jobs
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / India's mass incomes need small business growth, not just corporate jobsIndia's mass incomes need small business growth, not just corporate jobs

Prime Minister's message to India Inc to practise conscious capitalism is timely, but higher corporate wages alone will not move the needle on household incomes

premium

Representative image of corporate employees at a workplace in India

Rama Bijapurkar5 min read Last Updated : Nov 23 2026 | 10:15 PM ISTThe more frequent and richer employment data being put out by the government is truly welcome. Thank you Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation for your service and looking forward to more.  It informs the discussion on how widespread the impact on household income might be were Corporate India to pay its workers more. The larger message of the Prime Minister to India Inc to practise conscious capitalism is timely and relevant, especially as there is a slippage in consumer and societal trust in big companies the world over.  However, Corporate India’s wages impact a very small sliver of Indian households and workers, and the disconnected pools of work that India has does not make for transmission of this to the many Indias that we know exist. It will, of course, create some islands or islets of increased prosperity and boost their consumption and savings, but, by and large, will not affect the earnings of the bulk of households.  Government data shows that, of about 620 million workers, about 350 million are in non-agriculture sectors, and about 280 million of them are in small, informal enterprises with fewer than 20 workers. Of the 75 million who are formally employed, it is estimated that about 30 million are employed by the government. Government data shows that about 12 per cent of employment in India’s non-farm sector is accounted for by private companies.  By way of perspective, the information technology/tech industry employs around 6 million people, and private-sector banks employ about 850,000 people. Peruse this data any which way and the conclusion is pretty much the same. What happens to formal corporate-sector wages does not directly impact most households in the country, and will not move the needle on the incomes of most households because it does not have signalling value either.  The Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act set the floor for rural labour wages across the board forcing employers to match it or suffer the consequences. Government jobs, on the other hand, which pay higher salaries than private jobs have no such impact. Because of how limited these jobs are and the nature of the alternatives, young graduates, as is well known, are putting two to four years of their lives virtually on hold, or “in transit”, trying to pass competitive exams and get a well-paid government job with a predictable income. In the case of corporate jobs, even this access route does not exist.  If Corporate India were to pay its contractors more (since contract workers are the preferred option for low-skilled, labour-intensive work, in order to keep wages and headaches low), it might create some more islands of prosperity and fatten or lengthen the upper arm of the K-shaped income distribution that is so talked about nowadays. But for contractors, in turn, to share their increased income with the workers they hire is unlikely unless it is written into their contract — and it would sort of defeat the whole purpose of contracting out these activities in many cases. Minimum wage laws and better implementation are much more effective in raising worker incomes.   Eventually, higher household earnings come from increased economic activity that helps more people find more work and secure steady incomes, and from better skills that improve workers’ bargaining power and raise productivity, making employers want to pay more.  In the absence of more economic activity making better skilled jobs available, we see graduate unemployment rise and companies complain that they can’t find people for the jobs they have on offer. The push needed is to understand what it will take to get corporate India to invest big to seize the domestic market opportunity and the global opportunities that the new world is offering, with its fragmentation on one hand and the vastly improved perception — based on real demonstrated performance— of “made in India”.  As this column has often pointed out, the “no demand visibility” argument is tenuous, as is the low-capacity utilisation argument (maybe it’s the wrong kind of capacity, not producing at the price-performance point at which demand exists).  On the domestic front, the good news is that there is an even more pronounced attitude among mass-market customers of “stretch for more, not settle for less”, though the bad news is that incomes are still moving rather slowly upwards.  However, rural and urban mass-market consumers are now very similar in terms of exposure, attitudes and income, creating a mass market of enormous size. If large companies do not wish to pursue this customer, given the attractiveness of upper-income Consumer India, and if small businesses that do serve this customer currently have limits to expansion and innovation, then it is time for large companies to collect portfolios of small businesses and offer them what it will take policy a long time to do.  For large companies that have the appetite to invest in mass markets, the competitive advantage of muscle and tools (not consumer intimacy and innovation) that they could potentially have over small companies, coupled with the lack of similar sized competitors, could be a golden moment to grab. The government needs to start turbocharging its policies to help SMEs do better. For a start, detach the micro (M) from the SME and give each the tailor-made policy support that it needs.

entry.title: India's market rebound needs stronger growth to keep foreign investors
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / India's market rebound needs stronger growth to keep foreign investorsIndia's market rebound needs stronger growth to keep foreign investors

Foreign investors may be back, but India cannot afford to get distracted from the growth and reform agenda

premium

Illustration: Binay Sinha

Akash Prakash7 min read Last Updated : Nov 23 2026 | 10:07 PM ISTWhat a difference a month makes! From being ignored and at risk of irrelevance, India has come roaring back and how. In November, foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) have already pumped in $13 billion and the Indian markets are up about 15 per cent in dollar terms.  Given that Korea and Taiwan are down 15-20 per cent this month, we have seen a 3000-basis-point reversal in India’s underperformance in just 20 days. Breathtaking and also scary. The North Asian breakdown has been driven by the unwinding of the artificial intelligence (AI) trade, and is global in nature. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX) is down 42 per cent from its 2026 high and 25 per cent in the last month. Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix are down 45 per cent and 55 per cent, respectively, from their highs. The Nasdaq 100 is down 20 per cent from its high and 15 per cent in the last month. The Neoclouds have got decimated, with Coreweave down 78 per cent. FPIs are now scrambling to cover their India underweights, given the brutality and speed of the rotation away from North Asia. We see large-cap stocks in India starting to outperform.  India has benefitted from the AI selloff, but is this change in mood sustainable, or are we going to get whipsawed, with foreigners dumping the country again as soon as the AI trade is back in fashion? This is really the question. Is the change in mood on India more structural or purely tactical? How to think about this?  India is unlikely to attract the value-investor crowd. The markets are too expensive and even after 24 months of weak performance have not become cheap enough to attract the value buyer. At 18 times earnings, it is hard to call India cheap. Domestic flows, their quantum and stability, now over $50 billion per annum and growing, do not allow the markets to correct enough to become truly cheap. This dynamic is unlikely to change until such time as domestic flows reverse, which does not seem likely anytime in the near future.  So we remain a growth market. Investors come to India to buy companies that grow strongly and consistently. This is the attraction. Growth investors only care about the pace of earnings growth, its predictability and stability.  Most investors believe that India can deliver on a sustained basis 15-20 per cent earnings growth. The logic being nominal gross domestic product (GDP) grows at 12-13 per cent, the listed/organised sector grows faster and with some increase in profit share/ GDP, we can underwrite 15-20 per cent earnings growth.  There was also the belief that we can deliver this for an extended period of time and with little volatility. This was quite unique in the emerging market (EM) world. Multiples ultimately depend on earnings growth, and the predictability and stability of this growth. In a world of 3-3.5  per cent real GDP growth, 15 per cent earnings stands out. For context, the S&P 500 has delivered earnings growth at a compound annual growth rate of 7 per cent over the last 50 years. Thus, we got the valuation and attention that we did. At its peak, India accounted for over 20 per cent of the MSCI EM index and was the second-most expensive market in the world after the United States. Growth investors were all in and we had limited competition in attracting flows.  What has changed post-ChatGPT is that we are now seen as a loser of the AI buildout. If our competitive advantage of having an army of trained white-collar workers is no longer critical, is there a risk to investor growth assumptions? With our perceived weakness in innovation and the lack of cutting-edge technology, can we keep up with the anticipated surge in global productivity?  What if global investors can no longer underwrite a sustained 12-13 per cent nominal GDP growth or a non-volatile 15-20 per cent earnings trajectory? If one were to question the secular case for Indian earnings, then why pay such high multiples? Lower and more volatile growth will attract lower multiples and undermine the investment case.  What has also changed is that with the surge in AI-related capital expenditure (over $1 trillion in 2026 alone), earnings across the AI ecosystem have got supercharged. In 2026, earnings growth in the US is over 30 per cent, let alone Korea/Taiwan, which are clocking over 50 per cent. Investors believe that these elevated capex levels will continue and, therefore, so can the earnings. Again, why pay 18-20 times for India, which is growing earnings at only 15 per cent, when one can buy the US at similar multiples and Korea or the EM index at 10-12 times earnings when they are growing much faster?  With supercharged earnings across the world, the relative attractiveness of India’s 15 per cent growth has dimmed. Growth investors chasing earnings now have a choice! No one seems to care that for Korea/Taiwan or the US these are peak-of-the-cycle earnings.  For context, memory companies are currently reporting operating margins of 75 per cent. Indian earnings, not being driven by an AI buildout are not peak-of-cycle and, therefore, should be less volatile. You should obviously pay less for peak-of-cycle and highly volatile earnings as they will inevitably revert to the mean at some stage. For investors, growth is both faster and cheaper elsewhere.  India is impacted by the AI trade on two fronts, the willingness to believe in the structural nature of our growth and earnings as well as the relative attractiveness of a 15 per cent earnings trajectory.  Thus, whether the move back into India is sustained or not depends both on what we can do as a country to reinforce confidence in the India growth story, and on whether investors continue to believe in the AI buildout, its sustainability and monetisation.  The more investors believe in the structural growth of India and its earnings trajectory, the more they will be willing to pay. We need to accelerate the reforms momentum. There is genuine concern among many on India hitting a middle-income trap.  The more questions arise around the AI infrastructure buildout and its monetisation, the more investors will start normalising the supercharged current earnings of AI beneficiaries. Then, 15 per cent earnings will start looking very attractive again. India may also benefit from being seen as a beneficiary of the diffusion of AI and the broadening of use cases. The AI narrative may move away from just focusing on the infrastructure buildout.  We need both to happen for India to continue to attract foreign flows beyond the short-term catchup trade currently underway. Strengthening the case for India is the only part in our hands. We should not use the current inflows to lose focus on the steps we need to take to improve growth and productivity in India. To attract FPI capital in a sustained fashion requires the hard work of improving India’s structural growth potential. Absent that, the flows may come to hide from the current tech bloodbath but will not stay.

entry.title: COP31 climate talks expose deep divides over fossil fuels and finance
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / COP31 climate talks expose deep divides over fossil fuels and financeCOP31 climate talks expose deep divides over fossil fuels and finance

COP31's failure to reach a political agreement exposes deep divisions over fossil fuels and climate finance, putting global climate goals further at risk

premium

A COP31 sign is displayed at the venue of the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Turkey. (Photo: Reuters)

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 23 2026 | 10:01 PM ISTNo one was surprised when the 31st Conference of Parties (COP31) summit in Antalya, Turkey, ended without a central political agreement — the Antalya Pacts — despite running into two days of overtime. If anything, the longest-running climate talks in United Nations history highlighted the festering divisions between the developed and developing worlds over fossil fuels and climate finance. The result is that it is now clear that global temperatures are set to overshoot the Paris-Agreement target of holding temperatures below 1.5 degrees centigrade above pre-industrial levels — at a time when global temperatures broke new heat records this year. The draft pact sought to call on countries to keep the overshoot as low and for as short-lived a period as possible, a considerable dilution from the original Paris-Agreement pledges, and suggested carbon-capture storage as a substitute for cutting emission. The latter in itself is controversial; it works for some industries but is limited as an economically scalable solution.  But it was fossil fuels that proved a key deal breaker — although the pledge to transition away from fossil fuels was taken at COP28 in Dubai three years ago. The draft pact excluded all references to coal, oil and natural gas or transitioning away from fossil fuels, replacing it with anodyne phrasing on the “irreversible global transition towards low greenhouse gas emissions and climate-resilient development”. Refuting this framing was the European Union, the United Kingdom, Norway, small island-states and vulnerable states. This grouping was up against major oil- and gas-producing countries — most of them, not coincidentally, Turkish allies — as well as India, China, and Like Minded Developing Countries (LMDC). The other consequential point of disagreement was climate finance. A commitment to treble the figure by 2035 from $40 billion was articulated just last year. But the deepening North-South divide in climate talks means that the rich nations — the major historical contributors to global warming — were unwilling to commit to fixed contributions. At the same time, Russia accused developed nations of extending climate finance as loans rather than grants.  The 13 days of talks did record some gains, though the value of some of them is contestable. The proposed plan to raise electricity’s share in global consumption to 35 per cent by 2035 (the “35-by-35” deal) — which has morphed from a rigid mandate to a call for global cooperation — is one such. In countries such as China and India, for instance, the bulk of the electricity is generated through fossil fuels. At the same time, business deals worth $26 billion in agreements for renewables and grid pointed to some degree of momentum towards lowering greenhouse-gas emission. India’s low-key presence in Antalya reflected the shifting dynamics of climate talks. It continued to anchor its position in climate justice, Common But Differentiation Responsibilities and Respective Capabilities, equitable burden sharing, predictable finance for developing nation and an active opposition to climate-related trade barriers (such as Europe’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism). But it is notable that earlier this year, India withdrew its offer to host COP33 in 2028. As a result of the Antalya deadlock, many of the big issues will be carried over to COP32 in Addis Ababa next year.  Given the polarisation on the Turkish Riviera, consensus in a city on the edge of the Great Rift Valley looks just as unlikely.     Topics : Climate Change COP31 Global Warming Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment
